title: The Smartphone Revolution
summary: Discover how early devices like the IBM Simon and Apple's 2007 iPhone combined a phone, camera, and computer into one device that changed daily life.

versions.title: The Smartphone Revolution
versions.text:
A smartphone is a phone. It can do many things. It can take photos. It can play games. It can go on the web too.

Long ago, phones could call. That is all they could do. They could not take photos. They could not play games.

Then people made a new phone. This phone had a flat screen. You could tap it with one finger. It had no buttons at all.

This new phone could run small apps. One app took photos. One app told you the weather. One app sent notes to friends.

Today, these phones are everywhere. People use them to call and text. People use them to take photos. Many folks carry one phone each day.

versions.title: The Smartphone Revolution
versions.text:
A smartphone is a phone that can do many things. It can take photos. It can play games. It can go on the internet too. It can even help you find your way in a new city.

Long ago, phones could only make calls. They could not take any photos at all. They surely could not play any games.

Then people built a brand new phone to fix this. It had a touchscreen instead of buttons. You could tap the screen with your finger. There were no buttons left to press at all.

This new phone could run small programs called apps. One app could take clear photos fast. Another app showed the daily weather. Yet another app sent quick notes to friends.

Today, smartphones are found almost everywhere. People use them often to call, text, and take photos each day. Many people carry one phone wherever they go.

versions.title: The Smartphone Revolution
versions.text:
A smartphone is one phone that can do many things. It can take photos. It can play games. It can also connect to the internet. It can even help guide you around an unfamiliar city.

Long ago, mobile phones could only make simple calls. They could not take any photos at all. They surely could not play any games back then.

People later built a new kind of phone to solve this problem. This phone had a touchscreen instead of small, hard buttons. Users could tap the glass screen with a finger. There were no buttons left to press at all.

This new phone could also run small programs known as apps. One app took clear photos almost instantly. One app showed the daily weather. Yet another app sent quick notes to friends far away.

Today, smartphones can be found almost everywhere in the world. People use them to call, text, and take photos every day. Many people carry a smartphone wherever they go, from school to the local store.

versions.title: The Smartphone Revolution
versions.text:
A smartphone is one device that can do many things at once. It can take photos. It can play games. It can connect to the internet with ease. It can even help guide travelers around an unfamiliar city using a map.

Long ago, mobile phones were used only to make simple voice calls. They could not take photos, play games, or browse the internet at all.

People eventually designed a new kind of phone to solve this problem. This device had a touchscreen rather than small, hard buttons. Users could tap the glass screen with a finger to control everything. There were no physical buttons left on the front at all.

This new device could also run small programs known as apps. One app took clear photos almost instantly. One app showed the weather for any city. Yet another app let people send quick notes to friends far away.

Today, smartphones can be found in almost every corner of the world. People rely on them to call, text, browse, and take photos each day. Many people now carry one with them wherever they go, from early morning until late at night, no matter where they happen to be.

versions.title: The Smartphone Revolution
versions.text:
A smartphone combines a phone, a camera, a computer, and an internet connection into a single handheld device. For decades, mobile phones could only make voice calls. They could not take photographs, play games, or browse the internet.

In 1992, an early device called the IBM Simon introduced some of these same ideas. It had a touchscreen and basic built-in applications, including a calendar and a notepad. Still, it was bulky and expensive, so it never became popular. Then in 2007, Apple released the iPhone under the direction of its co-founder, Steve Jobs. It combined a touchscreen, a camera, internet access, and small programs called apps into one sleek, pocket-sized device.

The iPhone's design was controlled almost entirely through tapping and swiping a glass touchscreen rather than pressing physical buttons. This quickly inspired rival companies to build their own similar touchscreen phones. People soon began calling these new devices smartphones. Apps let people check the weather, navigate unfamiliar cities, and message friends instantly from nearly anywhere.

Within only a few years, smartphones transformed how people communicated, worked, and found information throughout their daily lives. Many people began reaching for a smartphone first thing each morning. They kept relying on it constantly throughout each day, at school, at work, and at home. Students used them to study, parents used them to stay in touch, and businesses used them to sell products and services online.

Today, smartphones remain central to daily life nearly everywhere on Earth. They are carried constantly by billions of people around the globe for calling, texting, photography, and endless browsing of news and entertainment. Engineers continue adding new features each year, from better cameras to faster internet connections, so the small devices in our pockets keep growing more capable and more useful with every single passing year that goes by.

keyWords.definition: the IBM Simon, an early touchscreen device released in 1992
keyWords.example: A museum display showed the bulky IBM Simon next to a modern smartphone.

keyWords.definition: a glass screen on a device that can be controlled by tapping and swiping with a finger
keyWords.example: He scrolled through his photos by swiping across the touchscreen.

questions.stem: What is the central idea of this passage?

options.text: the IBM Simon remained the most popular phone ever sold
the 2007 iPhone, building on earlier devices like the IBM Simon, transformed how people use phones in daily life
mobile phones have changed very little since the 1990s
Steve Jobs invented the very first mobile phone himself

questions.why: The passage traces how the iPhone, building on the earlier IBM Simon, transformed daily communication and phone use worldwide.

wrong.A: The passage says the Simon never became popular, unlike the iPhone.
wrong.C: The passage shows phones changed dramatically since the 1990s.
wrong.D: The passage credits earlier devices, not Jobs alone, with the first mobile phone.

questions.stem: According to the passage, in what year did the IBM Simon introduce an early touchscreen and built-in applications?
questions.why: The passage states that the IBM Simon appeared in 1992, introducing a touchscreen and basic applications.

wrong.B: The passage does not place the IBM Simon in 1987.
wrong.C: The passage does not place the IBM Simon in 2002.
wrong.D: The passage does not place the IBM Simon in 2010.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, who directed the release of the iPhone at Apple in 2007?

options.text: an engineer at IBM
an unnamed rival company
a government research team
Steve Jobs

questions.why: The passage specifically names Steve Jobs as the co-founder who directed the iPhone's release.

wrong.A: The passage credits Apple and Jobs, not an IBM engineer.
wrong.B: The passage names Apple, not an unnamed rival, as the creator.
wrong.C: The passage never mentions a government research team.

questions.stem: What can you infer about why the IBM Simon never became popular, despite having many of the same ideas as the iPhone?

options.text: it was never able to make voice calls at all
it came out several decades after the iPhone
it was likely too bulky and expensive for most ordinary consumers of its time
it used a design that no later phone ever copied

questions.why: The passage states the Simon remained bulky and expensive, which likely explains why few people bought it.

wrong.A: The passage never says the Simon could not make calls.
wrong.B: The Simon came in 1992, well before the 2007 iPhone.
wrong.D: The iPhone later copied the Simon's basic touchscreen idea.

questions.stem: What is most likely the reason rival companies quickly built their own touchscreen phones after the iPhone's release?

options.text: the iPhone's touchscreen design captured enormous public attention and clearly showed what was now possible
rival companies were legally required to copy Apple's design exactly
Apple asked other companies to help build iPhones
touchscreens had never before been used in any device

questions.why: The passage suggests the iPhone's popularity and design inspired competitors to build similar touchscreen phones of their own.

wrong.B: The passage never mentions any legal requirement to copy Apple.
wrong.C: The passage never says Apple asked rivals for help building iPhones.
wrong.D: The passage credits the IBM Simon with an earlier touchscreen.

questions.stem: What does the word 'fundamentally' mean as it is used in this passage?

options.text: only briefly and for a short period of time
in a way that is easily reversed later
in a manner that affects very few people
in a basic, essential, and far-reaching way

questions.why: In the passage, fundamentally describes a deep, essential change in how people communicated, worked, and found information.

wrong.A: Fundamentally does not mean brief in this passage.
wrong.B: Fundamentally does not mean easily reversed in this passage.
wrong.C: Fundamentally does not mean affecting only a few people.

questions.stem: How does the passage's structure help explain the smartphone's importance today?

options.text: it presents two opposing arguments about whether phones are helpful
it moves from the limits of early mobile phones, through the IBM Simon and the iPhone, to the device's current central role in daily life
it offers a step-by-step guide for coding a new app
it ranks several phone brands from best to worst

questions.why: The passage builds historical context from early limited phones through the iPhone, ending with today's widespread smartphone use.

wrong.A: The passage presents one historical account, not opposing arguments.
wrong.C: The passage does not provide app-coding instructions.
wrong.D: The passage never ranks specific phone brands.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what is a likely long-term effect of smartphones becoming so central to daily life?

options.text: engineers will keep adding new features, making future smartphones even more capable
fewer companies will try to build new smartphones in the future
smartphones will eventually stop being able to browse the internet
touchscreens will likely be replaced by physical buttons again

questions.why: The passage suggests ongoing improvements, such as foldable screens, will keep making smartphones more capable over time.

wrong.B: The passage shows rival companies kept building new smartphones.
wrong.C: The passage never suggests internet browsing will stop.
wrong.D: The passage never suggests a return to physical buttons.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how the IBM Simon and Apple's iPhone are connected, and why the iPhone's release in 2007 became such an important moment in the smartphone's history. Use details from the passage.
checklist: Explains that the IBM Simon in 1992 introduced an early touchscreen and built-in applications
Explains that Apple's iPhone, directed by Steve Jobs, combined a touchscreen, camera, and apps successfully in 2007
Connects the iPhone's popularity to rival companies building their own touchscreen smartphones afterward
HIGH.modelAnswer: In 1992, an early device called the IBM Simon introduced some of the same ideas later used in smartphones, including a touchscreen and basic built-in applications, although it remained bulky and expensive and never became popular. Then in 2007, Apple released the iPhone under the direction of its co-founder, Steve Jobs, combining a touchscreen, a camera, internet access, and small apps into one sleek, pocket-sized device. Unlike the Simon, the iPhone immediately captured widespread public attention, and its design, controlled almost entirely through tapping and swiping a glass touchscreen, quickly inspired rival companies to build their own competing touchscreen phones, which came to be known simply as smartphones. This moment mattered enormously because it set the pattern that nearly all modern phones still follow today.

LOW.stem: What would most likely happen if phones never got a touchscreen?

options.text: people would stop making phone calls completely
phones would become much smaller than before
apps would have been invented much earlier instead
people might still need buttons to use their phones

LOW.why: Without a touchscreen, phones might have kept needing buttons, since that is what touchscreens replaced.

wrong.A: The passage never suggests calls would stop completely.
wrong.B: The passage never connects touchscreens to phone size.
wrong.C: Apps came after the touchscreen, not before, in the passage.

LOW.stem: Why did the passage mention that old phones could not take photos or play games?

options.text: to prove that old phones were better than new phones
to explain why cameras are expensive to build
to show how different and limited old phones were compared to new phones
to argue that games should not be played on phones

LOW.why: This detail highlights how much phones changed once they gained new abilities like photos and games.

wrong.A: The passage actually favors the new phone's abilities.
wrong.B: The passage never discusses the cost of cameras.
wrong.D: The passage never argues against playing games on phones.

LOW.stem: How are the weather app and the photo app alike, based on the passage?

options.text: both are small programs that let the phone do one useful job
both are used only at nighttime
both were invented before the touchscreen phone
both require buttons instead of a screen

LOW.why: The passage shows both apps are small programs, each giving the phone a different useful ability.

wrong.B: The passage never says these apps only work at night.
wrong.C: Apps came after the touchscreen phone, not before.
wrong.D: The passage says apps run on the touchscreen, not buttons.

LOW.stem: What is the best reason the passage says smartphones are 'found almost everywhere'?

options.text: because smartphones are given away for free everywhere
because smartphones can only be bought in big cities
because every single app requires its own separate phone
because so many people now carry one with them every day

LOW.why: The passage explains that many people carry a smartphone with them wherever they go, which is why they are everywhere.

wrong.A: The passage never says smartphones are given away for free.
wrong.B: The passage never limits where smartphones can be bought.
wrong.C: The passage never says each app needs its own phone.

MID.stem: What would most likely happen if a phone could run no apps at all?

options.text: it would automatically browse the internet much faster
it would likely be limited to only a few basic tasks, like earlier mobile phones
it would need absolutely no touchscreen at all
it would become lighter than any smartphone sold today

MID.why: Without apps, a device would lose most of the added abilities the passage describes, much like the earlier simple phones.

wrong.A: The passage never claims fewer apps speeds up browsing.
wrong.C: The passage describes the touchscreen as essential to the device.
wrong.D: The passage never discusses the weight of such a device.

MID.stem: Why might the passage emphasize that this device let people 'control nearly everything' with a touchscreen?

options.text: to prove that touchscreens are completely impossible to damage
to suggest that older phones generally had more features overall
to highlight how differently this device worked compared to older phones with buttons
to argue that typing on a touchscreen is always much slower

MID.why: This detail emphasizes the major shift from button-based phones to a touchscreen controlling nearly everything.

wrong.A: The passage never claims touchscreens cannot be damaged.
wrong.B: The passage shows the new device had more features, not fewer.
wrong.D: The passage never compares typing speed between the two.

MID.stem: How are the new touchscreen device and the older mobile phones similar, based on the passage?

options.text: both are devices that cannot ever browse the internet
both were invented during the exact same single year
both run the same small programs that are called apps
both are devices that people use to make voice calls

MID.why: The passage shows both devices share the basic ability to make voice calls, even though the newer device can do much more.

wrong.A: The passage shows the new device can browse the internet.
wrong.B: The passage shows these devices were invented at different times.
wrong.C: Only the new device runs apps, according to the passage.

MID.stem: What is most likely the reason the passage describes several different apps, such as for weather and photos?

options.text: to show the wide variety of tasks a single smartphone can perform
to prove that each app requires its own completely separate device
to suggest that apps are rarely useful in everyday daily life
to argue that phones should only ever run one app at a time

MID.why: Describing several different apps helps show how many different tasks one smartphone device can now handle.

wrong.B: The passage shows apps run on one shared device, not separate ones.
wrong.C: The passage presents apps as very useful in daily life.
wrong.D: The passage never argues phones should run only one app.

HIGH.stem: What would most likely have happened if the IBM Simon had been cheaper and smaller in 1992?

options.text: it would have instantly stopped all future phone research entirely
it might have become more popular and perhaps changed phones sooner
it would have made voice calls completely impossible to place
it would have been banned from stores almost immediately

HIGH.why: Since cost and bulk likely limited the Simon's popularity, a cheaper, smaller version might have succeeded earlier.

wrong.A: The passage shows phone research continued after the Simon.
wrong.C: The passage never says the Simon could not make calls.
wrong.D: The passage never mentions any ban on the device.

HIGH.stem: Why might the passage specifically mention that Steve Jobs directed the iPhone's release rather than simply naming Apple alone?

options.text: to suggest that Jobs personally built every single iPhone by hand
to argue that Apple itself played no real role in the device
to highlight his personal role in shaping a device that changed communication
to prove that no one else at Apple contributed to the design

HIGH.why: Naming Jobs specifically credits his leadership in shaping a hugely influential invention, beyond just naming the company.

wrong.A: The passage never suggests Jobs built each phone by hand.
wrong.B: The passage credits Apple as the company releasing the device.
wrong.D: The passage does not rule out other contributors at Apple.

HIGH.stem: How does the IBM Simon compare with the iPhone, based on the passage?

options.text: both were released in the exact same year
both were designed by Steve Jobs personally
both failed to attract any public attention at all
both combined a touchscreen and built-in applications, but only the iPhone became hugely popular

HIGH.why: The passage shows the two devices shared key ideas, like a touchscreen, but only the iPhone achieved lasting popularity.

wrong.A: The passage places the Simon in 1992 and the iPhone in 2007.
wrong.B: The passage credits IBM, not Jobs, with the Simon.
wrong.C: The passage shows the iPhone captured widespread public attention.

HIGH.stem: What is most likely the author's purpose in writing this passage?

options.text: to explain how the smartphone developed into an essential part of daily life
to convince readers that Apple is a better company than IBM
to argue that mobile phones have caused more harm than good
to entertain readers with an invented story about Steve Jobs

HIGH.why: The passage traces the smartphone's historical development, aiming to inform readers about its growing importance in daily life.

wrong.B: The passage never ranks Apple as better than IBM overall.
wrong.C: The passage never argues phones caused more harm than good.
wrong.D: The passage presents real historical facts, not an invented story.
